sections.title: Front matter

summary.text: Opens a 2002 WHO information sheet on preventing HIV in infants and young children, describing mother-to-child transmission as the main route of infection and sub-Saharan Africa as the worst-affected region. It explains the timing and risk of transmission during pregnancy, delivery and breastfeeding and gives UNAIDS/WHO figures on children infected and dying in 2001.

sections.extract: Prevention of HIV in infants and young children A major public health problem HIV among children is a growing problem, particularly in the countries hardest hit by the AIDS epidemic. The overwhelming majority of infected children acquire the infection through mother-to-child transmission. Prevention of HIV infection in infants and young children is now a high priority and has been the rallying point for enhanced

sections.title: A public health solution that works

summary.text: Notes that mother-to-child HIV transmission has fallen below 2% in industrialised countries through antiretroviral drugs, elective Caesarean section and replacement feeding. It cites Thailand's fall in paediatric AIDS cases since prevention programmes began in 1997, alongside falling HIV prevalence among pregnant women.

sections.extract: The rate of transmission of HIV from infected pregnant women to their infants has decreased to less than 2% in industrialized countries through the use of highly effective antiretroviral drug regimens for the prevention of perinatal transmission (or for treating the mother) combined with elective Caesarean section and replacement feeding from birth. sections.title: The UNGASS Declaration of Commitment

summary.text: Quotes the 2001 UNGASS commitment to cut the share of infants infected with HIV by 20% by 2005 and 50% by 2010, with a chart of Thailand's declining paediatric AIDS cases. It begins listing needed interventions, starting with primary prevention of HIV among women, including during pregnancy and breastfeeding.

summary.text: Continues the list of interventions, calling for stronger family planning to prevent unintended pregnancies among women with HIV, most of whom do not know their status. It describes the package to prevent transmission to infants, including antiretrovirals, safer delivery, infant-feeding counselling and HIV testing, and stresses care and support for mothers and families.

sections.title: A framework for action to prevent HIV infection in infants and young children

summary.text: A framework diagram showing four levels of action: preventing HIV in all women, preventing unintended pregnancy and transmission to infants among women with HIV, and providing care and support.

sections.extract: All women prevent HIV infection HIV-infected women prevent unintended pregnancy HIV-infected women prevent transmission to infants and young children HIV-infected women, their infant and family provide care and support

sections.title: A comprehensive approach to prevent HIV infection in infants and young children

summary.text: Gives WHO estimates for Africa showing antenatal care coverage averaging 62% and professionally attended deliveries averaging 36%.

sections.extract: infants and young children Based on WHO estimates, the percentage of women receiving antenatal care, defined as at least one visit, ranges from 20% to 99% in Africa, with an average of 62%. The percentage of women having a pro- fessionally attended delivery ranges from 2% to 99%, with an average of 36%.

sections.title: Specific interventions to reduce mother-to-child transmission of HIV

summary.text: Describes specific interventions to reduce mother-to-child HIV transmission, including antiretroviral regimens chosen locally for feasibility, efficacy and cost, and safer delivery practices that limit invasive procedures. It gives infant-feeding advice: avoiding breastfeeding where replacement feeding is acceptable, feasible, affordable, sustainable and safe, and otherwise exclusive breastfeeding in the first months.

sections.extract: Antiretroviral drug use. A number of antiretroviral drug regimens – based on zidovudine, zidovudine and lamivudine or nevirapine, or combinations used in highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) – have been shown to be effective in reducing mother-to-child transmission of HIV. The choice of antiretroviral regimen should be made locally, taking into account issues of feasibility, efficacy and cost. Safer delivery

sections.title: More than the cost of drugs alone

summary.text: Argues that, although antiretroviral drug prices have fallen and donations have expanded access, weak health systems remain the main obstacle. Limited and late use of antenatal care and lack of HIV testing services still hinder delivery of prevention interventions.

sections.extract: For many years now, the cost of antiretroviral drugs has been seen as the key hurdle to implementing interventions that can prevent HIV infection in infants and young children in resource-constrained countries. sections.title: What WHO is doing

summary.text: States WHO's commitment to work with ministries, agencies, NGOs and people living with HIV to prevent HIV in infants, especially in the hardest-hit countries.

sections.extract: The task of helping countries prepare to engage in this effort is enormous, and WHO is committed to working with its traditional partners – ministries of health, international agencies, nongovernmental organizations and people living with HIV/AIDS – to make the prevention of HIV in infants a reality, especially in the hardest hit developing countries.

sections.title: Highlighting the importance of prevention

summary.text: States that WHO will keep its focus on preventing HIV among young women as the best way to protect infants.

sections.extract: WHO is committed to keeping the focus on the best and most humane ways to prevent transmission of HIV to infants and young children – that is, keeping young women free from infection. HIV prevention, in general, is a key focus for WHO’s Department of HIV/AIDS.

sections.title: Including HIV in family planning programmes

summary.text: Describes WHO's support for family planning programmes, including promoting dual protection against infection and pregnancy and greater use of male and female condoms.

sections.extract: Through the efforts of its Department of Reproductive Health and Research, WHO will build on its long history of supporting countries to improve the quality and coverage of their family planning and other reproductive health services. sections.title: Strengthening the infrastructure for preventing HIV infection in infants

summary.text: Outlines WHO's work to strengthen infrastructure for preventing HIV in infants, including expanding antenatal care through the Making Pregnancy Safer initiative and increasing access to voluntary counselling and testing. It stresses integrating prevention of infant HIV into national health systems.

sections.extract: Expanding antenatal care services. If preventing HIV infection in infants and young children is to be successful, women must have expanded access to antenatal care and must use the services more frequently and earlier in pregnancy than is currently the case. To address this issue, WHO will support maternal and reproductive health programmes in countries through its Making Pregnancy Safer Initiative. Increasing

sections.title: Increasing access to HIV care

summary.text: Notes that WHO is expanding access to HIV care in resource-limited settings and developing guidance on care, treatment and support for women identified through prevention programmes and their families.

sections.extract: WHO is intensifying efforts to increase access to HIV care in resource-limited settings, while strengthening linkages between prevention and care activities – to maximize the impact of both. Programmes for the prevention of HIV in infants and young children are identifying large numbers of women infected with HIV. WHO is developing guidance on key elements of a comprehen- sive approach to care, treatment and support

sections.title: Providing guidance

summary.text: Describes WHO's guidance role, including reviewing the science, advising on antiretroviral regimens for preventing transmission and treating HIV, and supporting safe infant feeding. It also mentions help for women with HIV to avoid unintended pregnancy and models to show where prevention investments are most cost-effective.

sections.extract: Keeping abreast of the science. WHO actively reviews developments in the science that underlies the prevention of HIV infection in infants and young children, assessing the strength of evidence and highlighting key gaps in the research base. This is an important service to countries, many of which do not have timely access to complete information on scientific developments and are thus at a disadvantage in

sections.title: Technical support to countries for a public health approach to prevention and

summary.text: States WHO's commitment to support a public health approach linking HIV prevention and care, followed by contact details for the WHO Department of HIV/AIDS and 2002 copyright.

sections.extract: care. WHO is committed to helping countries deliver both the best HIV prevention and the best HIV/AIDS-related care. In doing so, WHO hopes to elaborate the links and mutual benefits between prevention and care and to develop and strengthen a public health approach to confronting the AIDS epidemic in the future.
